authoredSolutions.33: Ethyl acetoacetate has both a ketone and an ester carbonyl. Under acidic conditions, ethylene glycol selectively protects the more electrophilic ketone as a cyclic 1,3-dioxolane (ketal); the ester is unaffected. So A is the ethylene ketal at the keto carbon. Hence option (B).
authoredSolutions.44: The reagent is \(HBr\) in \(CCl_4\). Markovnikov addition places \(H\) on the terminal \(=CH_2\), generating a secondary carbocation on the carbon next to the quaternary ring carbon. A 1,2-methyl shift then gives the more stable tertiary carbocation on the ring carbon (now bearing an isopropyl group), and \(Br^-\) attacks there. The major product is 1-bromo-1-isopropylcyclohexane. Hence option (D).
authoredSolutions.50: In an Ellingham diagram, the point where a line meets \(\Delta G = 0\) marks the equilibrium temperature, and a kink (sudden change of slope) marks a phase transition — melting or boiling — of the species. The indicated features therefore correspond to \(\Delta G = 0\) and melting or boiling. Hence option (A).

authoredSolutions.78: Pairing the integral with its image under \(x\to\frac{\pi}{2}-x\) (which swaps \(\sin\) and \(\cos\); the limits \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) and \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) are symmetric about \(\frac{\pi}{4}\)) gives \(2g(\alpha)=\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} 1\,dx=\frac{\pi}{6}\), so \(g(\alpha)=\frac{\pi}{12}\) — a constant independent of \(\alpha\). The feasible region is bounded by \(3x+4y\le 100\), \(4x+3y\le 75\), \(x,y\ge 0\). Both lines meet the \(y\)-axis at \((0,25)\), and \(4x+3y=75\) meets the \(x\)-axis at \((18.75,0)\), so the region is the triangle with vertices \((0,0),(18.75,0),(0,25)\). Since \(z=6xy+y^2\) is not linear, test the binding edge \(4x+3y=75\), i.e. \(x=\dfrac{75-3y}{4}\).
\[z=6y\cdot\frac{75-3y}{4}+y^2=112.5\,y-3.5\,y^2.\]
Maximise: \(\dfrac{dz}{dy}=112.5-7y=0\Rightarrow y=\dfrac{225}{14}\). Then
\[z=y\left(112.5-3.5y\right)=\frac{225}{14}\left(112.5-56.25\right)=\frac{225}{14}\cdot 56.25\approx 904.\]
This point \(\left(\tfrac{75-3y}{4},y\right)\) also satisfies \(3x+4y\le100\), so the maximum value of \(z\) is \(904\).

By continuity, \(\dfrac{1}{k}=f(0)=\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{\cos(\sin x)-\cos x}{x^{4}}\). Use \(\cos A-\cos B=-2\sin\dfrac{A+B}{2}\sin\dfrac{A-B}{2}\) with \(A=\sin x,\ B=x\):
\[\cos(\sin x)-\cos x=-2\sin\frac{\sin x+x}{2}\,\sin\frac{\sin x-x}{2}.\]
As \(x\to0\), \(\dfrac{\sin x+x}{2}\to x\) so \(\sin\dfrac{\sin x+x}{2}\approx x\); and \(\sin x-x\approx-\dfrac{x^{3}}{6}\) so \(\sin\dfrac{\sin x-x}{2}\approx-\dfrac{x^{3}}{12}\). Hence
\[\cos(\sin x)-\cos x\approx -2\,(x)\left(-\frac{x^{3}}{12}\right)=\frac{x^{4}}{6}.\]
Therefore the limit is \(\dfrac16\), so \(\dfrac1k=\dfrac16\Rightarrow k=6\).

Let \(P(E_1)=x,P(E_2)=y,P(E_3)=z\). Then \(\alpha=x(1-y)(1-z)\), \(\beta=(1-x)y(1-z)\), \(\gamma=(1-x)(1-y)z\), \(p=(1-x)(1-y)(1-z)\), so with \(a=\dfrac{x}{1-x},\ b=\dfrac{y}{1-y},\ c=\dfrac{z}{1-z}\) we get \(\dfrac{\alpha}{p}=a,\dfrac{\beta}{p}=b,\dfrac{\gamma}{p}=c\).
Divide \((\alpha-2\beta)p=\alpha\beta\) by \(p^{2}\): \(a-2b=ab\Rightarrow a=\dfrac{2b}{1-b}\).
Divide \((\beta-3\gamma)p=2\beta\gamma\) by \(p^{2}\): \(b-3c=2bc\Rightarrow c=\dfrac{b}{3+2b}\).
Since \(x=\dfrac{a}{1+a},\ z=\dfrac{c}{1+c}\), and \(1+a=\dfrac{1+b}{1-b},\ 1+c=\dfrac{3(1+b)}{3+2b}\),
\[\frac{x}{z}=\frac{a(1+c)}{c(1+a)}=\frac{\frac{2b}{1-b}\cdot\frac{3(1+b)}{3+2b}}{\frac{b}{3+2b}\cdot\frac{1+b}{1-b}}=6.\]
Thus \(\dfrac{P(E_1)}{P(E_3)}=6\).

\(\vec a\cdot\vec b=-\alpha\beta-\alpha\beta-3=-2\alpha\beta-3=1\Rightarrow \alpha\beta=-2\).
\(\vec b\cdot\vec c=-\beta+2\alpha+1=-3\Rightarrow 2\alpha-\beta=-4\Rightarrow \beta=2\alpha+4\).
Then \(\alpha(2\alpha+4)=-2\Rightarrow \alpha^{2}+2\alpha+1=0\Rightarrow(\alpha+1)^{2}=0\Rightarrow \alpha=-1,\ \beta=2\).
The scalar triple product is
\[(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec c=\begin{vmatrix}\alpha&\beta&3\\ -\beta&-\alpha&-1\\ 1&-2&-1\end{vmatrix}=\alpha^{2}-\beta^{2}+\alpha+5\beta.\]
Substituting \(\alpha=-1,\beta=2\): \(1-4-1+10=6\). Hence \(\dfrac13\big((\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec c\big)=\dfrac{6}{3}=2\).

\(\det A=(2)(-1)-(3)(0)=-2\), so \(\det(A^{4})=(\det A)^{4}=(-2)^{4}=16\).
For \(2\times2\): \(\operatorname{Adj}(2A)=2\,\operatorname{Adj}(A)=2\begin{bmatrix}-1&-3\\0&2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2&-6\\0&4\end{bmatrix}\).
Both \(A\) and \(\operatorname{Adj}(2A)\) are upper triangular, so their \(10\)th powers have diagonals
\[A^{10}:\ (2^{10},(-1)^{10})=(1024,1),\qquad (\operatorname{Adj}(2A))^{10}:\ ((-2)^{10},4^{10})=(1024,4^{10}).\]
The difference is upper triangular with diagonal \((1024-1024,\ 1-4^{10})=(0,\,1-4^{10})\), so
\[\det\!\left(A^{10}-(\operatorname{Adj}(2A))^{10}\right)=0\cdot(1-4^{10})=0.\]
Total \(=16+0=16\).

The upper limit is \(\sqrt{\pi/2}\approx1.2533\), and since \([x^{2}]\) is an integer, \(\big[[x^{2}]-\cos x\big]=[x^{2}]+[-\cos x]\).
For \(x\in[0,1)\): \([x^{2}]=0\) and \(\cos x\in(\cos1,1]\subset(0,1]\Rightarrow[-\cos x]=-1\), so the integrand \(=-1\).
For \(x\in[1,\sqrt{\pi/2}]\): \(x^{2}\in[1,\pi/2)\Rightarrow[x^{2}]=1\), and \(\cos x\in(0,1)\Rightarrow[-\cos x]=-1\), so the integrand \(=0\).
Hence
\[\int_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi/2}}\big[[x^{2}]-\cos x\big]dx=\int_{0}^{1}(-1)\,dx+\int_{1}^{\sqrt{\pi/2}}0\,dx=-1.\]
The required value is \(|-1|=1\).

Circle 2: \(x^{2}+y^{2}-24x-10y+160=0\) has centre \(C_2=(12,5)\), \(r_2=\sqrt{144+25-160}=3\).
Distance between centres: \(C_1C_2=\sqrt{(12-5)^{2}+0^{2}}=7\).
Since \(r_1+r_2=6<7\), the circles are separate, so the minimum distance is
\[C_1C_2-r_1-r_2=7-3-3=1.\]

The required plane belongs to the family
\[(2x-7y+4z-3)+\lambda(3x-5y+4z+11)=0.\]
At \((-2,1,3)\): first bracket \(=-4-7+12-3=-2\); second \(=-6-5+12+11=12\). So \(-2+12\lambda=0\Rightarrow\lambda=\tfrac16\).
Multiply through by \(6\):
\[6(2x-7y+4z-3)+(3x-5y+4z+11)=0\Rightarrow 15x-47y+28z-7=0.\]
Thus \(a=15,\ b=-47,\ c=28\), and
\[2a+b+c-7=30-47+28-7=4.\]
